name: Dana Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and work weekend calls and chats at a contact centre. I finished secondary school and I'm still slow on overlapping refund cases, so I'm junior even though the weekend rate is good. I use the approved AI summariser every day, then check the ledger myself before telling a caller what they'll get back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What matters when you leave work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works at a furniture warehouse. We have two children, six and thirteen, a mortgage and ten months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other centres near us. I like trying new tools, but I don't count a tool as correct just because it makes a neat sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the approved summariser helps me find what a caller asked last week. It doesn't decide whether a disputed payment is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like that my job stays recognisable. I'm still junior at disputed payments, but the weekend rate is good and our household has ten months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the weekend queue and use the summariser each day, checking every amount against the account ledger. In the first year I'll keep a short log of wrong summaries and add to savings from any extra shift, if one is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, though I still feel a jolt when two account entries clash. A quiet year gives me time to learn the ordinary job better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your household still owe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner works at a furniture warehouse and our children are six and thirteen. We paid down the house steadily, but the mortgage still comes every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake changed how you use the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once saw the summariser treat a late refund as a new charge. I look at the ledger before I let a neat sentence become a promise.

say: I'd say **summaries** help find past questions faster, provided an agent still checks the customer's record.
I'd keep **payment decisions** tied to the account ledger.
think: I feel **secure** with good weekend pay and ten months saved.
I still need practice on **disputed payments**.
do: Keep handling **weekend calls** during the first year.
Check **AI summaries** against the ledger every day.
Save from **extra shifts** only if those hours are offered.
feel: **Calm**, with normal nerves on disputed payments.
S0.quote: I look at the ledger before I let a neat sentence become a promise.
fieldNote: Her **weekend rate** explains higher pay despite junior status.
She uses **AI daily**, but catches errors in the payment ledger.
Her **ten-month reserve** is real while the mortgage remains monthly.

steps.text: Keep taking weekend customer calls and checking AI summaries
Save part of extra-shift wages if new hours are offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should test the new answer system on missed refunds before it handles live calls. I want junior agents to see the error count, not just a slide saying it saves time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the weekend queue could shrink before I become good at unusual claims. Ten months saved helps us wait for a sound offer, but other centres may adopt the same system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask to join the paid pilot and compare thirty old refund chats with the machine's answers. If my weekend hours fall in the first year, I'll apply for posted paid service-testing jobs nearby only if the offered wages and hours cover our mortgage; I'll keep my present shift until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but curious enough to test it. I can make a plan; I cannot make the centre keep every junior seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check your results?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask another agent to check the thirty cases without seeing my notes. Then we'd compare the missed refunds at the next team meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the new job need to offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A test job must say what the paid hours are and how many cases an agent owns. I wouldn't move for a title if the weekend pay loss leaves a hole in the mortgage budget.

say: I'd test **missed refunds** before live calls move to software.
I'd share **error counts** with junior agents, not just speed claims.
think: I may lose the **weekend queue** before mastering unusual claims.
I know **other centres** may shrink their junior seats too.
do: Compare **thirty old chats** in the paid pilot this month if accepted.
Present **missed-refund counts** with another agent at the team meeting.
Seek **posted paid testing work** after cuts only at mortgage-covering hours and wages; keep current shifts until an offer is signed.
feel: **Anxious and curious** while the weekend roster could shrink.
S1.quote: I can make a plan; I cannot make the centre keep every junior seat.
fieldNote: She seeks **independent checking** from another agent on her test.
The **weekend premium** matters in any offer comparison.
Her **strong reserve** buys time but cannot guarantee nearby vacancies.

steps.text: Compare thirty old refund chats with AI during an approved paid pilot
Apply for posted paid testing work after cuts only if wages and hours cover mortgage
Keep present weekend shifts until a mortgage-covering offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues general AI by 2028 could settle the disputes I am still learning. Robots around 2031 come later for hands-on jobs; the delay doesn't help our calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior place could go, including the weekend hours that pay well. Ten months saved gives us time, but my partner's warehouse wage alone will not cover the mortgage and both children indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll keep a record of false refund answers without customer names and ask for written staffing dates. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for advertised paid care-assistant work only if the wage and hours cover the mortgage; I won't pay for a course without a real opening that requires it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not frozen. The fast date makes me protect the reserve instead of treating it like spare cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in your household budget first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner the weekend pay might stop and show the household figures. We would postpone the new sofa before using our mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is care work a safe escape?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Care work is hands-on now, but robots could change it around 2031. I'd ask to see an actual paid shift and its duties before calling it my next career.

say: I'd say **2028 AGI** could take our dispute calls.
I'd explain **2031 robots** do not delay headset losses.
think: I expect my **junior weekend role** could disappear.
I know **ten months saved** cannot replace both wages forever.
do: Log **false refund answers** without customer details starting now.
Apply for **advertised paid care work** after a real cut only if hours and wages cover mortgage.
Postpone the **new sofa** before using the mortgage reserve.
feel: **Anxious**, with a buffer but no guaranteed next job.
S2.quote: The fast date makes me protect the reserve instead of treating it like spare cash.
fieldNote: Her **ten-month reserve** supports a search, not an open-ended transition.
She knows **care work** may change when hands-on robots arrive.
She keeps **course spending** behind an actual required paid opening.

steps.text: Apply for advertised paid care work after a cut only if wages and hours cover mortgage
Postpone buying the new sofa before touching mortgage savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us test which tasks still need people and give juniors paid time to learn. Thinking AI reaches our calls in 2031; hands-on robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become good at checking unusual claims by 2031, though the same general AI might do that work. A paid care shift would tell me more than a career poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll take supervised practice on old refund cases during my paid weekend shift and ask the care home about a paid trial day. If it posts a paid vacancy with wages and hours covering our mortgage, I'll try the day; in the first year after 2031 I'll apply only if the written offer still meets those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but interested. Five years is enough to test the care work without quitting a good wage on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see lifting, cleaning and the early start, not only pleasant visits. I'd ask whether the home expects robots to change those tasks around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you arrange the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would arrange school pickup before a trial day. I would not use up both our wages just to test a job, so the trial must be paid.

say: I'd ask for **paid junior practice** over five years.
I'd separate **2031 call risk** from robots around 2034.
think: I might improve at **unusual claims** before AGI arrives.
I would test **paid care work** before treating it as household income.
do: Practise **old refund cases** on my paid weekend shift.
Take a **paid care trial** only for a mortgage-covering posted vacancy after arranging school pickup.
Apply for a **posted paid care job** only if written wages and hours cover mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy but interested** with time to test a real shift.
S3.quote: A paid care shift would tell me more than a career poster.
fieldNote: She wants the **physical duties** visible before a career move.
Her **school pickup** and two wages constrain trial timing.
She sees **2034 robots** as a later risk to care tasks.

steps.text: Keep taking paid weekend calls while practising old refunds
Take paid care trial after arranging school pickup for a posted mortgage-covering vacancy
Apply for posted paid care work only with written mortgage-covering wages and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets workers gather proof of skill and compare actual wages before switching fields. General AI reaches our calls in 2036, while hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still owe on the mortgage, but the children will be older. I could spend the years improving claims and testing care work without surrendering weekend pay today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep my weekend calls, practise hard refunds and save part of every extra shift if extra hours are offered. I'll check posted paid care roles twice a year; in the first year after 2036 I'll move only if my call hours fall and a written offer covers our mortgage and school travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the decade, though not blind to the end point. One paid experiment at a time feels possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you build a bigger reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to hold a full year of expenses, but only from pay we actually receive. If the weekend premium dries up, we'll slow the savings target rather than borrow to meet it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to ask for the wage and hours beside any training course. A good plan still needs a pay packet.

say: I'd compare **posted wages** and hours before changing fields, especially while our weekend rate pays well.
I'd distinguish **2036 call work** from robots around 2039.
think: I may still have a **mortgage** at 53.
I can test **care work** while weekend pay continues, without treating a trial as a guaranteed job.
do: Keep my **weekend calls** and practise hard refunds.
Save from **extra shifts** only when paid hours are offered.
Move after 2036 only if **calls shrink** and a written paid offer covers mortgage and school travel.
S4.quote: A good plan still needs a pay packet.
fieldNote: Her **one-year reserve goal** depends on real extra shifts.
The **written offer** must cover both housing and school travel.
She prefers **paid experiments** while keeping a strong current wage.

steps.text: Keep taking paid weekend calls while practising difficult refunds
Save part of offered extra-shift pay toward one year of expenses
Move after 2036 only if calls shrink and written paid offer covers mortgage and travel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It could remove my weekend calls before I am good at complex refunds, and nearby centres might all cut at once. Written notice and a posted paid care opening with enough hours for the mortgage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the customer can correct an AI answer without starting over. A refund mistake grows each time somebody copies it into a new chat. That problem still needs an owner.

headlineQuote: A refund mistake grows each time somebody copies it into a new chat.
portrait: Dana is a **43-year-old junior agent** with secondary schooling, still learning overlapping refunds on weekend shifts.
Her **weekend rate** brings higher pay, and her family has ten months saved alongside a mortgage and two school-age children.
She uses **AI daily** and checks it against the ledger; many other contact centres are nearby.
The **2028 date** worries her most, while longer timelines let her test paid care work before later hands-on robots arrive.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her well-paid weekend calls while nearby centres make similar cuts.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** would show when the weekend wage is at risk.
A **posted paid care role** with mortgage-covering hours would permit a careful move.
